facts.claim: Bilinguals did not show a reduced n-1 shift cost and did not show an enhanced n-2 repetition cost compared to monolinguals in one task-switching experiment.
facts.quote: However, we did not observe such results. Our findings suggest that previous results cannot be replicated and that the n-2 repetition cost is another index that shows no reliable bilingualism effect.

facts.claim: The prefrontal cortex (PFC) can be used to quantify and classify mental workload with up to 78% accuracy for single-trial discrimination of three levels of workload.
facts.quote: The results show up to 78% accuracy for single-trial discrimination of three levels of workload from each other.

facts.claim: A higher rate of everyday language switches was related to a smaller mixing cost in errors in a set shifting task.
facts.quote: Most consistent effects were found for the set shifting task where a higher rate of everyday language switches was related to a smaller mixing cost in errors.

facts.claim: Bilinguals demonstrated a smaller mixing effect (global switch cost) than monolinguals, indicating better ability to reconfigure stimulus-response associations.
facts.quote: Monolinguals and bilinguals performed similarly when switching between tasks (local switch cost) in a mixed-task block, but bilinguals demonstrated a smaller mixing effect (global switch cost) than monolinguals

facts.claim: Participants in a high load condition walked more slowly and performed the counting task more slowly and with more errors than those in the low load condition.
facts.quote: Participants in the high load condition walked more slowly and performed the counting task more slowly and with more errors than those in the low load condition.

facts.claim: Concussed adolescents exhibited a significantly greater switch cost on the Task-Switching Test (P = 0.038, mean difference value = 38 ms) compared to control subjects.
facts.quote: Compared with control subjects, the concussed group exhibited a significantly greater switch cost on the Task-Switching Test (P = 0.038, mean difference value = 38 ms)

research.angle: While high mental workload and certain types of task switching are linked to increased prefrontal cortex activity and errors, the evidence on whether these habits consistently reduce functional IQ or provide a general executive advantage is mixed and inconsistent.
research.verdict: The sources show that multitasking and task-switching increase prefrontal cortex workload and can lead to more errors, but they do not provide a definitive measure of a functional IQ drop.
research.caveat: The studies vary significantly in methodology, ranging from small-scale fNIRS experiments to observational studies on head trauma and bilingualism.
